title: Senior's toolkit: browser-side defences
summary: DevTools for cookies and CSP violations, CSP Evaluator, report-only roll-outs with reporting endpoints, curl preflights, and the encoders and sanitizers that do the real work.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: browser-side defences
steps.body: Browser-side bugs are found in the browser and fixed in headers and templates. These are the tools to see what the browser actually does, and the APIs that make the fix boring.

toolkit.cmd: DevTools → Application → Cookies, and the Console
toolkit.what: See every cookie with its HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite flags; the Console and the Issues panel show each CSP violation and each cookie the browser refused or blocked, with the reason.
flags: Origin, Sec-Fetch-Site and the CORS answer
toolkit.example: Refused to execute inline script because it violates the following Content Security Policy directive: "script-src 'nonce-...' 'strict-dynamic'"

toolkit.what: Ship a policy that only reports. Violations go to a reporting endpoint (Reporting-Endpoints + report-to), so you see what would break before anything does.
flags: the older form, still widely supported
toolkit.example:
Reporting-Endpoints: csp="https://shop.example/csp-reports"
Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: script-src 'nonce-{n}' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; report-to csp

toolkit.what: Paste a policy and get each weakness explained: host allow-lists with known bypasses, 'unsafe-inline' without a nonce, missing object-src or base-uri.
toolkit.example: script-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com  ->  "Host allowlists can frequently be bypassed"

toolkit.what: Test a CORS policy the way a browser does, with any origin you like. Try your SPA, evil.example, null and a look-alike, with and without credentials.
toolkit.example: for o in https://app.shop.example https://evil.example null; do curl -s -o /dev/null -D - -H "Origin: $o" https://api.shop.example/api/me | grep -i '^access-control-allow-origin' || echo "$o: none"; done

toolkit.what: Encode for the context on output (System.Text.Encodings.Web); when users must send HTML, sanitize it with an allow-list library on the server (HtmlSanitizer) or in the browser (DOMPurify).
flags: keep <b> and <a>, drop scripts and handlers
the same in the browser, before innerHTML
toolkit.example: var safe = new Ganss.Xss.HtmlSanitizer().Sanitize(review.Body);   // then Html.Raw(safe) is acceptable

steps.prompt: Match each tool to the question it answers.
pairs: Is the session cookie HttpOnly and SameSite?
What would this policy break if we enforced it?
Does this policy have a known bypass?
Does the API trust sandboxed pages?
How do we keep users' bold text without their scripts?

steps.prompt: Check whether the API reflects an arbitrary origin.
A new CSP goes straight to enforcing on Friday and the checkout's payment widget stops loading. What should the roll-out have looked like?
options: Report-only first, watch the reports for a week, fix the violations (nonces, moving inline handlers), then enforce with reporting still on
Add 'unsafe-inline' and * to script-src and enforce
Put the policy in a <meta> tag so it can be removed quickly
